senses.gloss:
Mithilā
(‘where enemies are routed’)
------------------------------------------
Mithilā has been a well-known city in the epics and the पुराणस्. This was where the king जनक (Vaideha or Sīra-ध्वज), ड़थेर् of सीता, lived and ruled over his kingdom, the Videha. It was built by the king Mithi, grandson of इक्ष्वाकु.
It is sometimes identified with Janakpur in Uttar Pradesh near Nepal border. Others think it is Tirhut in Bihar.
The epics and the पुराणस् have described it as a grand and majestic city.

mithyā
(‘that which upsets or confuses the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
The words ‘mithyā’ and ‘mithyājñāna’ are widely used in the अद्वैत वेदान्त दर्शन. If ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, is the one and only Reality, the one without a second (tathya; eka; advitīya), then, all else that appears to exist—this world and the innumerable beings in it—must be मिथ्या, unreal and false. To think that the world is real, that the body-मिन्द् complex is itself the आत्मन् or the Self, is mithyājñāna or false knowledge.
The reason for this is अविद्या or अज्ञान (nescience) which, at the cosmic level, is called māyā. It is anādi (without beginning) but can be ended with विद्या or ज्ञान (true knowledge of the आत्मन्/ ब्रह्मन्).
See also AVIDYĀ.
The Brahmavaivartapurāṇa describes मिथ्या as the wife of अधर्म. Her brother is Kapaṭa (deceit). These two are invisible in the Kṛta or सत्य yuga, appear in a subtle form in the त्रेतायुग, half manifest in the द्वापरयुग and fully manifest, creating havoc in the कलियुग.
Obviously this is a symbolic way of describing the gradual increase of falsehood and deceit over the four epochs.
